title: State Central Library (Asafia)
description: State Central Library (Asafia) in Hyderabad: founded in 1891, moved to Afzal Gunj in 1936, its public-library role, manuscript heritage, and relationship to Telangana’s manuscript institutions.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Hyderabad · Established 1891 · Afzal Gunj since 1936

items.value: About 500,000 books and magazines reported by Government of India

blocks.intro: The State Central Library is one of Hyderabad’s major surviving public institutions from the Asaf Jahi period. Government sources place its establishment in 1891 and identify its earlier name as the Asafia Library. The institution later moved to the large Afzal Gunj building on the Musi, where it became the apex public library of the state.

sections.sub: The library began during the reign of the sixth Nizam
body: Government accounts date the library to 1891. India Cine Hub attributes its establishment to the efforts of scholar-administrator Moulvi Syed Hussain Bilgrami, also known as Nawab Imad-ul-Mulk Bahadur, and states that his personal books formed an important part of the initial collection.<cite data-ref="india-cinehub-scl"></cite>

The Hyderabad district government describes the State Central Library as the largest public library in the state and places it among the institutions that shaped the city’s literary development.<cite data-ref="hyderabad-district"></cite>

sections.sub: The purpose-built library belongs to the later Asaf Jahi modernization of Hyderabad
body: The present Afzal Gunj building represents a later phase of the institution. India Cine Hub records that its foundation stone was laid in January 1932 under Mir Osman Ali Khan and that the Asafia Library moved into the completed building in 1936.<cite data-ref="india-cinehub-scl"></cite>

Its scale—large halls, high ceilings and a prominent riverside position—gave the library a civic presence different from a private manuscript collection. The move turned the institution into a visible part of Hyderabad’s twentieth-century public architecture.

sections.sub: The institution’s importance lies in access as well as preservation
body: Government of India material reports roughly half a million books and magazines in the State Central Library and describes it as the apex of the state library system. The collection includes material in several languages associated with Hyderabad’s multilingual intellectual life.<cite data-ref="india-cinehub-scl"></cite>

That public role distinguishes the State Central Library from specialist archives. It is not merely a heritage building or manuscript repository; its historical importance also comes from the idea that a major princely-state collection could become a public reading institution serving the city and, later, the state.

sections.title_html: A history shared with Telangana’s manuscript institutions
sections.sub: The Asafia name links several later preservation histories
body: The Telangana Government Oriental Manuscripts Library and Research Institute traces its own institutional origins to the 1891 library and records the growth of a large manuscript collection in Urdu, Arabic, Persian and other languages before later administrative reorganizations created a dedicated manuscripts institution.<cite data-ref="tgomlri-history"></cite>

This means the Asafia legacy should not be described as though every manuscript associated with the old library remains physically in one modern institution. The more accurate picture is a shared institutional history: the public State Central Library and the specialized manuscripts institute both inherit parts of Hyderabad’s longer project of collecting, preserving and making knowledge available.<cite data-ref="tgomlri-history"></cite>
